title: Schemas, Validation & Quarantine
objective: After this lesson you will be able to design a target schema for extracted data, write validators returning per-row error lists, quarantine rejects with reasons instead of dropping them, and report reject rates as a process metric.
why: Extraction produces strings; systems need records — typed fields, required keys, bounded formats. Without a schema, garbage enters quietly and explodes downstream ('why is revenue NaN?'). Validation-first means every reject carries a reason, rejects never vanish silently, and the reject rate becomes the pipeline's health metric instead of a shameful secret.

blocks.text: A **schema** declares what each record must hold: field names, types, required flags, format rules (email shape, date range, enum membership). Write it before cleaning a single value — schemas turn arguments ('is this row usable?') into checks. Keep schemas small and explicit: five strict fields beat twenty aspirational ones nobody enforces.

blocks.caption: Five fields, typed, with presence and format rules — the whole contract

blocks.text: A validator returning `true/false` destroys information. Return **error lists**: every violated rule as a message naming field + expectation + actual value. Error lists power quarantine reports, rule tuning ('80% of rejects are one bad date format → fix the parser'), and stakeholder conversations ('here is exactly what failed and why').

blocks.caption: Coercion happens once, centrally, visibly — never scattered across callers

blocks.text: Quarantine: rejects with reasons, never silent drops

Invalid rows go to **quarantine**: stored with their errors, counted, reported — never deleted, never silently fixed. Quarantine serves three masters: auditability (prove what entered and what didn't), tuning (reject patterns reveal parser bugs vs source rot), and recovery (fixed rules re-process quarantined rows). A pipeline without quarantine is a pipeline that lies about its input.

blocks.caption: Two streams out, reject rate as the headline metric

blocks.title: Reading the reject rate
blocks.text: Low-but-nonzero with categorized reasons = healthy pipeline. 0% = validators asleep (or no validation at all). 40% = schema fights reality — loosen rules or fix extraction, don't hand-edit rows. Sudden jumps between runs = source format changed; the quarantine diff tells you exactly how.

blocks.title: Quarantine the batch
blocks.note: Run it: expect 2 clean, 2 quarantined — one format mismatch, one missing-email (required) + below-minimum. Every reject names its reasons; that list is the quarantine report.

items: Schema first: types, presence, formats — interpretation before repair
Validators return error lists (field + expectation + actual), never bare booleans
Quarantine stores rejects with reasons: auditability, tuning signal, recovery path
Reject rate is the health metric: low-nonzero healthy, 0% asleep, floods mean schema-vs-reality mismatch

exercise.prompt: Extend the practice schema with a required name (minLen 2) and an optional country. (a) Run five rows through it in the playground: two clean, one missing name, one bad email, one negative hours. (b) Write the quarantine summary: counts + distinct error messages. (c) State which single validator change would halve the rejects, and whether that change is a fix or a surrender.
hints: Copy the practice validator, add name rule { type: 'string', required: true, minLen: 2 } (needs the minLen check from the lesson's full version) and country { required: false }.
Five rows: clean ×2, missing-name ×1, bad-email ×1, negative-hours ×1 → expect 2 clean / 3 quarantined with 3 distinct messages.

Halving rejects usually means relaxing one rule (e.g. making email optional) — a surrender unless evidence shows the rule misfires on good data. Fixes change parsers; surrenders change standards: name which yours is.
exercise.why: The fix-vs-surrender distinction is the senior judgment this lesson exists to teach: every relaxed rule is a standard lowered, and standards lower only on evidence of misfiring — never to beautify a metric.

quiz.q: Validator returns true/false instead of error lists. What is lost?
options: Quarantine reasons, tuning signal, and stakeholder evidence: why each row failed, which rules misfire, proof of diligence
quiz.explain: Booleans discard the diagnosis. Error lists turn rejects into actionable reports — the difference between '3 rows failed' and '3 rows failed, all on email format, parser suspected'.

quiz.q: Reject rate jumps from 2% to 40% overnight. First move?
options: Diff the quarantine: new error messages reveal what changed upstream (usually source format drift) — fix parser or rules, never rows
quiz.explain: Sudden jumps mean the world changed, not the code. The quarantine diff names the change; hand-editing rows treats symptoms while corrupting auditability.

quiz.q: 0% reject rate across 10,000 messy PDF rows means?
options: Validators asleep or absent — messy sources always produce rejects; zero means nothing is being checked
quiz.explain: Real extraction is lossy; zero rejects on messy input proves non-enforcement. Healthy pipelines show low-but-nonzero with categorized reasons.

summary: Schema declares, validators explain (error lists), quarantine preserves (reasons + counts), reject rate reports health. Validate first, clean second, drop nothing silently.
